title: Mean Value Theorem
body:
> If $f$ is [[Continuity|continuous]] on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then there is some
> $c$ in $(a,b)$ with
> $$f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$$

Somewhere in the interval, the **instantaneous** rate of change equals the **average** rate of
change over the whole interval. Drive 100 km in one hour and at some instant your speedometer read
exactly 100 km/h. Geometrically: some tangent line is parallel to the secant joining the endpoints.

**Rolle's theorem** is the special case $f(a) = f(b)$, where the secant is horizontal and the
theorem says $f'(c) = 0$ for some $c$. The general case is Rolle applied to $f$ minus that secant
line.

Like the Intermediate Value Theorem it is an **existence** result: it promises $c$ is there and
gives you no way to find it. Its job is not computation, it is licensing.

## What it licenses

Every "the sign of the derivative tells you the behaviour on an interval" claim in
[[Curve Sketching]] and [[Optimization]] is a corollary of this theorem, and without it they are
guesses:

- $f' = 0$ everywhere on an interval $\Rightarrow$ $f$ is **constant** there
- $f' > 0$ everywhere $\Rightarrow$ $f$ is increasing there
- two functions with the same derivative differ by a constant, which is where the $+C$ in an
  indefinite [[Integral]] comes from and why it is the *only* freedom

It also bounds the error of a [[Linear Approximation]], and is the step in the proof of the
[[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] that connects the two halves of the course.
